newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul investors calm as biggest-ever strike looms.
newsitem.headline: Seoul investors calm as biggest-ever strike looms.

text.p: Trading on South Korea's stock market was calm on Monday despite plans for the country's biggest strike in history, but brokers said investors would remain cautious until the industrial crisis was solved.
Some manufacturing-dependent blue chips -- which have been most affected by the worker unrest -- even posted gains due to bargain hunting, brokers said.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions has called out its 1.2 million members on Tuesday for a two-day strike to try to force the government to dump a new labour law which allows firms to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
They will be joined on Wednesday by members of the 500,000-strong Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has vowed an indefinite walkout against the law.
"Strikes were the major factor but investors were calm, rather guessing on the market's trend after the crisis," said Park Byung-moon, head of sales at LG Securities.
The market finished at exactly the previous session's closing level of 659.54 points, after fluctuating mildly between 655.74 and 664.95.
Chipmaker Samsung Electronics Co gained 2.33 percent to 44,000 won and carmaker Hyundai Motor Co climbed 1.79 percent to 22,700 won.
Brokers said many investors were optimistic that a last-minute solution, or at least some indication of an early settlement, to the stoppages could be reached.

Brokers also said the market consolidated following four consecutive days of rises led by banks and other financial stocks on speculation that mergers and acquisitions would become active in the financial sector.
That speculation followed President Kim Young-sam's remarks last week that a panel would be set up to oversee restructuring of the financial industry. Details have yet to be drawn up.
"Banks and brokerages were the first targets for consolidation as they were the first to spark the rally," said Yoo Nam-gil, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
The broader financial sub-index dropped 1.33 percent while the sub-index for banks fell 1.74 percent.

An overhang of loans used for margin trading since the middle of last year continues to dampen sentiment on the market, already hit by a slowdown in the economy that is expected to cut into corporate earnings for 1996.

Such loans have fallen to 2.59 trillion won ($3.05 billion) from about 2.8 trillion won since late last year while customer deposits with brokerages have risen to 2.57 trillion won from around 2.4 trillion won, analysts said.
They said sentiment should improve as deposits catch up with margin loans.
